title: "Decision Trees"
body-classes: fam-tree
---

[**Tree family**]{.fam-badge} · the interpretable non-parametric classifier that splits the feature space into axis-aligned boxes — and the high-variance building block every [ensemble](ensembles.qmd) is made of. Siblings: [Random Forests](random_forests.qmd) and [Ensembles](ensembles.qmd) (average / boost many trees to tame the variance), [Logistic Regression](logistic.qmd) and [LDA](lda.qmd) (linear boundaries instead of axis-aligned cuts), [kNN](knn.qmd) (the other non-parametric local learner).

## 1. Essence

A decision tree predicts by asking a sequence of simple yes/no questions about one feature at a time — "is petal width ≤ 0.8?", then "is petal length ≤ 4.95?" — until it reaches a leaf, where it returns the majority class of the training points that landed there. It is built by **recursively partitioning** the training set: starting from the whole sample at the root, the algorithm searches every feature and every candidate threshold, picks the single split that makes the two resulting subsets as **pure** (class-homogeneous) as possible, and then repeats the same procedure on each subset until a stopping rule fires (Lecture 4, slides 9–10/11). The result is a flowchart you can read top-to-bottom, which is the method's headline selling point.

It is a **non-parametric** model: it commits to no functional form and no fixed number of parameters, so it can carve out arbitrarily complex, **axis-aligned** decision regions and capture non-linearities and interactions automatically — no scaling, no encoding, no linearity assumption (Lecture 4, slide 9/11). That flexibility is also its weakness. Grown unchecked, a tree will keep splitting until every leaf is pure, **memorizing the training data**; and because each split depends on the one above it, a tiny change in the data can flip an early split and reshape the whole tree — trees are **high-variance and unstable** (Lecture 4, slide 9/11; Lecture 7, slide 15/21).

Compared with its nearest neighbors: a single tree is the **baseline** that [Random Forests](random_forests.qmd) and [Ensembles](ensembles.qmd) exist to improve on — they grow *many* trees and average (bagging) or stage (boosting) them to cancel out that variance. Against the [linear](logistic.qmd) classifiers, a tree draws **staircase** boundaries (perpendicular cuts) where [Logistic Regression](logistic.qmd) and [LDA](lda.qmd) draw a single straight line — a tree wins when the true boundary is blocky or interaction-heavy, and loses (needing a deep, jagged staircase) when it is genuinely linear. Like [kNN](knn.qmd) it is non-parametric and makes local decisions, but a tree's regions are learned splits rather than distance to stored points.

## 2. When to use / when *not* to use

::: {.callout-intuition}
**Reach for a decision tree when…**

- You want a **fully interpretable** model you can read as a flowchart and show a non-technical stakeholder — the path from root to leaf *is* the explanation (Lecture 4, slide 9/11).
- Features are a **mix of types and scales** (numeric, ordinal, categorical) and you'd rather not standardize or one-hot-encode — trees split on thresholds, so **no feature scaling is needed** (Lecture 4, slide 9/11).
- The relationship is **non-linear with interactions** and you don't want to hand-engineer terms — recursive splitting captures curvature and "feature A matters only when feature B is high" for free.
- You need a **fast, transparent baseline** before reaching for the heavier machinery. On the Spring-2025 exam's breast-cancer task (Assignment 3), a single tree is exactly that baseline before [Random Forests](random_forests.qmd) and gradient boosting (see [§7](#sec-tree-exam)).
:::

::: {.callout-pitfall}
**Reach for something else when…**

- **Predictive accuracy and stability matter more than reading a single tree** → a lone tree overfits and is high-variance. Bag it into a [**Random Forest**](random_forests.qmd) or stage it with [**gradient boosting**](ensembles.qmd) — that is the entire reason those methods exist, and exactly the progression the exam asks for ([§7](#sec-tree-exam)). The [depth curve in §5](#sec-tree-viz) shows the overfitting symptom directly.
- **The true boundary is essentially linear** → [**Logistic Regression**](logistic.qmd) or [**LDA**](lda.qmd) capture it with one smooth boundary, whereas a tree needs a deep, jagged staircase of axis-aligned cuts to approximate a diagonal line (and overfits doing so).
- **The data is small and noisy** → tree structure is **unstable**; a few flipped points can rebuild the tree (Lecture 7, slide 15/21). Prefer a lower-variance model or, again, an ensemble.
- **You need smooth probability estimates or "+1 unit ⇒ +β" effect sizes** → a tree's leaf probabilities are piecewise-constant and coarse; use a [linear](logistic.qmd) model for calibrated, interpretable coefficients.
:::

## 3. Code idiom {#sec-tree-code}

The canonical course idiom is `scikit-learn`'s `DecisionTreeClassifier` from `sklearn.tree`, paired with `plot_tree` to render the flowchart. The course uses **sklearn only** here — there is no from-scratch tree in the lecture notebooks.

**The default tree — fit, score, inspect size** *(notebook `07_Decision_trees.ipynb`, cell 7)*:

```python
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

clf = DecisionTreeClassifier()        # all defaults: criterion='gini', max_depth=None (grow until pure)
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
clf.score(X_test, y_test)             # accuracy on the held-out 30%
clf.get_depth(); clf.get_n_leaves()   # how big did the unconstrained tree grow?
```

**Choosing the split criterion, and pre-pruning to fight overfitting** *(notebook `07_Decision_trees.ipynb`, cells 12, 13, 16)*:

```python
DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion='gini',    random_state=0)   # default criterion (Gini impurity)
DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion='entropy', random_state=0)   # entropy ≡ information gain

# Pre-pruning: require ≥5 training samples in every leaf → shallower, simpler tree
clf_pruned = DecisionTreeClassifier(min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=0)
clf_pruned.fit(X_train, y_train)
```

Every hyperparameter, annotated. `criterion` selects the impurity measure — **`'gini'` is the default** (slightly cheaper to compute), `'entropy'` uses information gain ([§8](#sec-tree-math); the two usually give very similar trees). `random_state` fixes the tie-breaking among equally-good splits, so set it for reproducibility. The **stopping / pre-pruning** knobs all default to "grow until pure": `max_depth=None` (no depth cap), `min_samples_split=2`, `min_samples_leaf=1`, `min_impurity_decrease=0.0`. Tightening any of them — e.g. `max_depth=3` or `min_samples_leaf=5` — shrinks the tree and trades a little training fit for lower variance. In practice you **tune these by cross-validation** (`GridSearchCV`), which is exactly what the exam's Assignment 3.3 asks for ([§7](#sec-tree-exam)).

::: {.callout-pitfall}
**A default tree overfits — and watch the leaf-count comment trap.** With `max_depth=None` the tree splits until every leaf is pure, so **training accuracy goes to 100% while test accuracy peaks early and then sags** (the [§5 depth curve](#sec-tree-viz) shows this on real WDBC data). Always pre-prune (`max_depth` / `min_samples_leaf`) or, better, ensemble. Two implementation traps from notebook 07 worth flagging so you don't copy them blindly: (i) cell 17 builds the "pruned" tree with **`min_samples_leaf=10`** even though the surrounding comment *and* the plot title both say "5" — quote the **actual** value `10` if you lift it [NB-1]; (ii) cells 12, 13 and 17 fit on the **full `X, y`** (for a complete-looking picture) rather than on `X_train` — only cells 7 and 16 use the train/test split, so don't read those full-data trees as held-out evaluations [NB-1].
:::

## 4. Worked examples

### Example 1 — a default tree on Iris, and the size it grows to {#sec-tree-iris}

The course's running example is the **Iris** dataset (150 flowers, 3 species, 4 features), loaded from the UCI URL with a 70/30 split (`random_state=0`) *(notebook `07_Decision_trees.ipynb`, cells 4, 7)*. An **unconstrained** `DecisionTreeClassifier()` fit on the 105 training flowers:

```python
clf = DecisionTreeClassifier().fit(X_train, y_train)
clf.score(X_test, y_test)   # 0.9778
clf.get_depth()             # 4
clf.get_n_leaves()          # 7
```

scores **test accuracy ≈ 0.978** (44/45 correct) with a tree of **depth 4 and 7 leaves** *(computed via the course `.venv`, reproducing nb07 cell 7; `random_state=0`)*. Iris is nearly linearly separable on petal measurements, so even a default tree generalizes well — but note it still grew to 7 leaves on 105 points, fitting some of the training-set detail it didn't need. The tree's `feature_importances_` confirm the intuition: **`petal_width` carries ≈ 0.92** of the importance and `sepal_length` exactly `0.0` — the tree never splits on it (computed). That is decision-tree feature selection happening for free, and the kind of ranking Assignment 3.7 asks for on the breast-cancer data.

### Example 2 — Gini vs entropy, and pre-pruning the tree {#sec-tree-prune}

Re-fitting with each split criterion *(notebook cells 12, 13)* — both on the same data — produces trees of **identical size: depth 5, 9 leaves** for Gini *and* for entropy (computed via `.venv`). This is the practical face of [disagreement R9-1](#sec-tree-math): Gini and (log₂) entropy are different formulas but rank candidate splits almost identically, so they usually yield the same tree — the course notebook says as much ("both often yield similar results, although `gini` is somewhat faster", nb07 cell 2).

Now **pre-prune**. Requiring at least 5 samples per leaf *(notebook cell 16, on the train split)* collapses the tree from depth 4 to **depth 3 with 5 leaves**, but here test accuracy *drops* to **0.911** (computed) — on an already-easy problem, pruning bought simplicity at a small accuracy cost rather than a gain. (The notebook's *next* cell, 17, then builds a tree with **`min_samples_leaf=10` fit on the full `X, y`** — depth 4, 6 leaves — and mislabels it "min_samples_leaf=5"; that is the [NB-1] code/comment mismatch from [§3](#sec-tree-code), and the depth-4 figure is over the whole dataset, not a held-out score.) The lesson: pruning is a **variance-reducing** move — it earns its keep when the unpruned tree is overfitting, which Iris barely does but WDBC clearly does ([Example 3](#sec-tree-wdbc)).

### Example 3 — a single tree as the WDBC baseline (exam Assignment 3) {#sec-tree-wdbc}

The Spring-2025 exam's Assignment 3 classifies the **Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer** data (`wdbc.data`: 569 tumors, 30 real-valued nucleus features, target malignant `M` / benign `B`, 357 B / 212 M) and walks up the tree family: **single tree → [Random Forest](random_forests.qmd) → gradient boosting** (`phase0/exam_spring2025_notebook.md`). The single tree is step 3.3 — the baseline the ensembles must beat. With a stratified 75/25 split (`random_state=1`):

```python
df = pd.read_csv("wdbc.data", header=None)        # col 1 = diagnosis, cols 2: = 30 features
X, y = df.iloc[:, 2:].values, df[1].values
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=1)

tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=1).fit(Xtr, ytr)
tree.score(Xtr, ytr)   # 1.000  ← memorized the training set
tree.score(Xte, yte)   # 0.923
```

An unconstrained tree hits **train accuracy 1.000 but test accuracy 0.923** (depth 7, 18 leaves) — the train–test gap is the **overfitting fingerprint** in plain sight (computed via `.venv`). Tuning the complexity by 5-fold cross-validation (Assignment 3.3) selects `max_depth=5` with CV accuracy ≈ 0.944 and test accuracy ≈ 0.909 — barely different on the test set, because **a single tree's variance can't be cross-validated away, only ensembled away** (computed). That is precisely why the exam continues to Random Forests and boosting (3.4–3.6): the [§5 depth curve](#sec-tree-viz) shows the test accuracy plateauing around 0.92 no matter how deep you grow, while a forest of such trees pushes it higher.

::: {.callout-bigpicture}
This is the setup where [**Random Forests**](random_forests.qmd) and [**Ensembles**](ensembles.qmd) earn their keep, and why the exam pairs the single tree with them: a tree is a *high-variance, low-bias* learner, so **averaging many decorrelated trees** (bagging / RF) slashes the variance at almost no bias cost. See the [classification showdown](../cross_method/showdowns.qmd) for Tree vs RF vs Gradient Boosting on this same WDBC data.
:::

## 5. Visualization {#sec-tree-viz}

The one figure that earns its place for a decision tree is the **overfitting curve**: training and test accuracy as the tree is allowed to grow deeper. It makes the family's defining failure mode visible — training accuracy climbs monotonically to a perfect 1.0 as the tree memorizes, while test accuracy peaks early and then *stops improving* (here it plateaus; on noisier data it would decline). The gap that opens between the two lines **is the variance** that [Random Forests](random_forests.qmd) and [Ensembles](ensembles.qmd) are built to close. The data below is computed on the real WDBC exam dataset (75/25 stratified split, `random_state=1`).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: fig-tree-depth
//| fig-cap: "Decision-tree overfitting curve on the WDBC breast-cancer data (computed via the course .venv, 75/25 stratified split, random_state=1). x-axis: max_depth of the tree; y-axis: accuracy. The green line is training accuracy — it climbs straight to 1.0 by depth 7 as the tree memorizes the 426 training tumors. The grey line is test accuracy — it peaks at depth 2–3 (≈0.93) and then plateaus around 0.92 no matter how much deeper the tree grows. The widening gap between the two lines is the tree's variance: extra depth buys training fit but not generalization. This is exactly why the exam moves on to Random Forests and boosting."
famTree = (getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue('--family-tree').trim() || "#06A77D")
depthData = [
  {depth: 1,  train: 0.9225, test: 0.8951},
  {depth: 2,  train: 0.9648, test: 0.9301},
  {depth: 3,  train: 0.9718, test: 0.9301},
  {depth: 4,  train: 0.9859, test: 0.9091},
  {depth: 5,  train: 0.9953, test: 0.9091},
  {depth: 6,  train: 0.9977, test: 0.9161},
  {depth: 7,  train: 1.0000, test: 0.9231},
  {depth: 8,  train: 1.0000, test: 0.9231},
  {depth: 9,  train: 1.0000, test: 0.9231},
  {depth: 10, train: 1.0000, test: 0.9231}
]
tidy = depthData.flatMap(d => [
  {depth: d.depth, accuracy: d.train, set: "training"},
  {depth: d.depth, accuracy: d.test,  set: "test"}
])
Plot.plot({
  height: 320, marginLeft: 55, marginRight: 80, grid: true,
  x: {label: "max_depth (tree complexity →)", domain: [1, 10]},
  y: {label: "Accuracy", domain: [0.85, 1.01]},
  color: {domain: ["training", "test"], range: [famTree, "#777"], legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(tidy, {x: "depth", y: "accuracy", stroke: "set", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot(tidy, {x: "depth", y: "accuracy", fill: "set", r: 3}),
    Plot.text(tidy.filter(d => d.depth === 10), {x: "depth", y: "accuracy", text: "set", dx: 10, fontSize: 11, fill: "set"})
  ]
})
```

(The other natural figure is the **flowchart itself** — `plot_tree(clf, filled=True, feature_names=..., class_names=...)` from nb07 cells 12/13/17 — which renders the splits and leaf classes; it's the static artifact you'd put in an exam write-up to explain a model.)

## 6. Diagnostics & interpretation

What to report and inspect to judge a decision tree:

- **Train vs test accuracy** — the headline. A perfect (or near-perfect) **train** accuracy with a clearly lower **test** accuracy (WDBC: 1.000 vs 0.923) is the overfitting/variance fingerprint. Compare across `max_depth` (the [§5 curve](#sec-tree-viz)) to find where test accuracy stops improving.
- **Tree size — `get_depth()` and `get_n_leaves()`** — a deep tree with many leaves relative to the sample size is memorizing. Pre-pruning (`max_depth`, `min_samples_leaf`) shrinks both; report them before and after.
- **`feature_importances_`** — total impurity decrease attributed to each feature (sums to 1). This is the tree's interpretation output: which features drive the splits (Iris: `petal_width` ≈ 0.92; nb07 cell 19 suggests inspecting it). It *ranks* drivers but, unlike a [linear](logistic.qmd) coefficient, gives no sign or "+1 unit ⇒ +β" reading.
- **The plotted tree** — read root-to-leaf paths as decision rules; the root split is the single most informative threshold. Watch for leaves built on very few samples (high-variance predictions).
- **Stability check** — refit on a slightly different split or bootstrap; if early splits change, the tree is unstable (Lecture 7, slide 15/21), a direct cue to ensemble.

::: {.callout-bigpicture}
Comparative diagnostic vs siblings: a single tree gives you a *readable rule set* and *impurity-based feature importances* but **noisy, high-variance predictions**; a [**Random Forest**](random_forests.qmd) trades the readable rules for *averaged, low-variance predictions* and *more reliable* (permutation or impurity) importances. Choose the diagnostic that matches the question: "show me the rule" → single tree; "rank the drivers and predict well" → forest.
:::

## 7. Past-exam lens {#sec-tree-exam}

::: {.callout-exam}
**How decision trees show up — as the baseline of the tree family.** In the **Spring-2025 take-home (Assignment 3, on `wdbc.data`)**, the single decision tree is **step 3.3**: load and stratify-split the breast-cancer data, fit a tree, **use cross-validation on the training set to choose a complexity constraint** (e.g. `max_depth` / `min_samples_leaf` via `GridSearchCV`), refit, and report test performance (`phase0/exam_spring2025_notebook.md`). It is then the reference that **[Random Forest](random_forests.qmd) (3.4)** and **gradient boosting (3.5)** must beat, with 3.6 asking you to *compare all three through the bias–variance lens* and 3.8 asking *why an ensemble can beat a single tree* — the tree's high variance is the answer. Expect to (i) write the `DecisionTreeClassifier` idiom from [§3](#sec-tree-code); (ii) **tune complexity by cross-validation** and justify the chosen depth; (iii) report and interpret the **train–test gap as variance**; and (iv) read off `feature_importances_` (3.7 asks this for the forest). The grade rests on the *reasoning* — explaining why the ensemble improves on the single tree — at least as much as the code.
:::

## 8. Math {#sec-tree-math}

::: {.math-section}
::: {.math-off-hint}
*Math is off. Use the **Math** toggle in the top bar to show the course-level derivation (and "full" for the rigorous version).*
:::

::: {.callout-math-a}
**Mode A — course level.** The course defines a decision tree by its **impurity measures** and the **information gain** a split achieves *(Lecture 4, slides 10–11/11; notebook `07_Decision_trees.ipynb` cell 2)*. For a node $S$ with class proportions $p_i$ over $C$ classes, the two measures are the **Gini index**
$$G(S) = \sum_{i=1}^{C} p_i\,(1-p_i) = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{C} p_i^2$$
— the chance of misclassifying a point if you label it by drawing a class at random in proportion to $p_i$ — and the **entropy**
$$H(S) = -\sum_{i=1}^{C} p_i \log_2 p_i ,$$
the information-theoretic uncertainty of the node. Both equal $0$ for a perfectly pure node (all points in one class) and are maximal at the uniform split. Training (slide 10/11) is greedy: at each node search every feature and threshold and keep the split that maximizes the **information gain** — the impurity reduction from parent to the size-weighted children,
$$\text{IG} = I(\text{parent}) - \sum_{\text{children }k} \frac{n_k}{n}\, I(\text{child}_k),$$
where $I$ is $G$ or $H$, $n_k$ is the count in child $k$ and $n$ the parent count — recursing until a stopping rule fires (max depth, min samples, or impurity gain below a threshold). **Log base [disagreements R9-1]:** the course slide and notebook write entropy with **$\log_2$** (bits), kept as primary here; the reference texts (ESL §9.2, ISL §8.1) write the same node measure as cross-entropy/deviance with the **natural log**, $-\sum_k \hat p_{mk}\log \hat p_{mk}$. The two differ only by the constant factor $\ln 2$, which **cannot change the argmax split**, so Gini and entropy rank candidate splits almost identically — the practical consequence shown in [§4 Example 2](#sec-tree-prune) (Gini and entropy give the same-size tree). Foundations in the [math appendix](../appendix/math_appendix.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-math-b}
**Mode B — full rigor.** *(Anchored to ESL §9.2 "Tree-Based Methods", eqs 9.10–9.17.)* ESL frames the tree as **CART** — recursive binary partitioning of the feature space into rectangles $R_1,\dots,R_M$, predicting a constant in each (ESL §9.2.1):
$$f(x) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} c_m\, I(x \in R_m) \qquad \text{(ESL 9.10).}$$

**Regression trees (ESL §9.2.2).** Under squared-error loss the best constant in a region is the node mean, $\hat c_m = \operatorname{ave}(y_i \mid x_i \in R_m)$ (ESL 9.11). Finding the globally optimal partition is infeasible, so CART is **greedy**: at a node, a candidate split on variable $j$ at point $s$ defines the half-planes $R_1(j,s)=\{X\mid X_j \le s\}$ and $R_2(j,s)=\{X\mid X_j > s\}$ (ESL 9.12), and we choose $(j,s)$ to minimize the within-child sum of squared error,
$$\min_{j,\,s}\Bigl[\, \min_{c_1}\!\!\sum_{x_i \in R_1(j,s)}\!\!(y_i-c_1)^2 \;+\; \min_{c_2}\!\!\sum_{x_i \in R_2(j,s)}\!\!(y_i-c_2)^2 \,\Bigr] \qquad \text{(ESL 9.13),}$$
whose inner minimizers are the two child means (ESL 9.14). The split point $s$ is found by scanning the inputs; the process recurses on each child.

**Cost-complexity pruning (ESL §9.2.3).** Rather than stop early (short-sighted, since a weak split can enable a strong one below it), grow a large tree $T_0$ — stopping only at a minimum node size — then prune. For a subtree $T \subseteq T_0$ with $|T|$ terminal nodes, write $N_m = \#\{x_i \in R_m\}$, $\hat c_m = \tfrac{1}{N_m}\sum_{x_i \in R_m} y_i$, and the node cost $Q_m(T) = \tfrac{1}{N_m}\sum_{x_i \in R_m}(y_i-\hat c_m)^2$ (ESL 9.15). The **cost-complexity criterion** trades fit against size,
$$C_\alpha(T) = \sum_{m=1}^{|T|} N_m\, Q_m(T) + \alpha\,|T| \qquad \text{(ESL 9.16),}$$
with tuning parameter $\alpha \ge 0$. For each $\alpha$ there is a unique smallest minimizing subtree $T_\alpha$, found by **weakest-link pruning** (successively collapse the internal node giving the smallest per-node increase in $\sum_m N_m Q_m$), and $\hat\alpha$ is chosen by five- or ten-fold cross-validation. At $\alpha=0$ the solution is the full $T_0$; larger $\alpha$ collapses toward the root. (sklearn exposes this as `ccp_alpha`.)

**Classification trees (ESL §9.2.3).** Only the node measure changes. With $\hat p_{mk} = \tfrac{1}{N_m}\sum_{x_i\in R_m} I(y_i=k)$ the class proportions in node $m$, ESL gives three node-impurity measures $Q_m(T)$ (ESL 9.17):
$$\text{misclassification error: } 1-\hat p_{mk(m)}, \quad \text{Gini: } \sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat p_{mk}(1-\hat p_{mk}), \quad \text{cross-entropy/deviance: } -\sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat p_{mk}\log \hat p_{mk},$$
where $k(m)=\arg\max_k \hat p_{mk}$ is the majority class. The Gini and cross-entropy forms are **differentiable** and more sensitive to changes in the node proportions than misclassification rate, so ESL recommends them for *growing* the tree and any of the three for *pruning*. The Gini index has a tidy reading: code each observation $1$ for class $k$ and $0$ otherwise; its node variance is $\hat p_{mk}(1-\hat p_{mk})$, and summing over $k$ recovers Gini. **[R9-1]** carries over: this is ESL's natural-log deviance, the same measure as the course slide's $\log_2$ entropy up to the factor $\ln 2$.

**Instability (ESL §9.2.4).** ESL stresses that trees are **high-variance**: a small change in the data can change the top split, whose effect propagates to every split below — the price of estimating a simple, hierarchical structure. This is exactly the variance term of the bias–variance decomposition (stated, not re-derived, in the [math appendix](../appendix/math_appendix.qmd#sec-biasvar)), and the reason ESL points to **bagging** (§8.7) — averaging many trees — to reduce it, the bridge to [Random Forests](random_forests.qmd) and [Ensembles](ensembles.qmd).
:::
:::
